memory_leads.lead: China's WTO-era industrialization, steel output and infrastructure boom drove a powerful increase in seaborne iron ore, coal and other bulk demand, lifting tonne-miles and supporting a historic dry-bulk earnings boom.

memory_leads.lead: The Baltic Dry Index rose to extraordinary levels before collapsing in 2008, becoming a widely watched symbol of the shipping/commodity supercycle and then of the financial crisis.
unknowns: How market participants interpreted the index at each stage

memory_leads.lead: Chinese shipbuilding capacity expanded rapidly, joining South Korea and Japan as a major commercial shipbuilding center; yards and new entrants chased the order boom across bulkers, tankers and containerships.
High freight earnings, cheap credit and rising vessel prices encouraged aggressive ordering and leverage, creating a very large newbuilding pipeline just before the global financial crisis.
unknowns: Share funded by KG, banks, public equity or private owners

memory_leads.lead: Container trade growth remained strong with China's export integration, global sourcing and just-in-time supply chains; carriers ordered progressively larger ships and developed broader logistics/terminal footprints.
Liner conferences weakened or were abolished in important jurisdictions while carrier alliances and vessel-sharing agreements became more important mechanisms for network coordination.
Very large containership design accelerated, while the later fuel-price spike and 2008 downturn helped make slow steaming a major operating response to save fuel and absorb excess capacity.
unknowns: Fuel versus capacity-management rationale by carrier

memory_leads.lead: Chinese container ports such as Shanghai, Shenzhen and Ningbo rose rapidly, while Singapore, Hong Kong and other established hubs faced changing rankings; global terminal operators expanded cross-border concession portfolios.
Tanker markets experienced their own China/oil-demand and fleet-cycle volatility, while double-hull replacement continued reshaping the fleet and older single-hull tonnage approached phase-out.
LNG liquefaction capacity and LNG-carrier ordering accelerated materially, with Qatar and other large projects expanding fleet demand; specialized propulsion and containment technologies evolved.

The global financial crisis caused an abrupt collapse in trade, freight rates, ship finance and asset values; dry bulk was especially dramatic, while container lines faced severe overcapacity and losses.
Traditional shipping banks and German KG structures came under intense stress as vessel values fell and charter coverage deteriorated, setting up a long post-crisis deleveraging/restructuring cycle.
Somali piracy surged around the Gulf of Aden/Indian Ocean, increasing security costs, rerouting risk, naval intervention and onboard protection debates.
unknowns: Industry judgment on armed guards at the time

memory_leads.lead: Environmental regulation broadened beyond oil pollution toward air emissions, ballast water and efficiency concerns; the shipping industry's greenhouse-gas debate became more visible before the 2010s rules hardened.

judgment_leads.judgment: A strong supercycle thesis likely argued that China's commodity and trade growth would keep vessel demand ahead of supply despite heavy ordering.
judgment_leads.outcome_boundary: Do not let the 2008 crash erase how plausible structural-demand optimism looked before the shock.

judgment_leads.judgment: Owners, yards and lenders likely differed on whether record asset prices and freight rates represented durable scarcity or a late-cycle bubble amplified by financing and port congestion.
judgment_leads.outcome_boundary: Reconstruct competing views before the crisis.

judgment_leads.judgment: Post-Lehman expectations likely ranged from a short inventory/trade shock to a multi-year balance-sheet and overcapacity depression.
judgment_leads.outcome_boundary: Later Chinese stimulus and recovery must not be backdated.

judgment_leads.judgment: Container carriers increasingly viewed slow steaming as both a fuel-saving measure and a way to absorb surplus ships, though service and inventory costs created tradeoffs.
judgment_leads.outcome_boundary: Do not infer later normalization of slow steaming into the original rationale without evidence.
